newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe split on calls for Albania military mission.
newsitem.headline: Europe split on calls for Albania military mission.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers, searching for a response to Albania's self-destruction, were divided on Saturday on whether to back calls for military intervention.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said his country, the current OSCE president, was in favour of having the international community put together a force.
But British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told reporters as he arrived for an informal meeting in the Dutch countryside it was "premature" to think about such a move.
Germany has also said it was sceptical about the international community sending peacekeeping troops.
Sweden's Lena Hjelm-Wallen was blunt about the EU's predicament. "Frankly, we don't know what to do," she told reporters.

Ministers from across the 15-nation bloc were meeting for what was supposed to be a relaxed chat about plans for expanding into the former communist areas of central Europe, but were forced by events on their eastern borders to focus on Albania.
OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Friday there was no alternative to foreign intervention to halt Albania's descent into chaos.

His call was echoed by Carl Bildt, the international community's Bosnia representative, who said in a statement that Europe's failure to act would make current discussion on joint foreign and security policy look "pathetic".
The EU has been seeking to present a more coherent face in foreign policy to go along with its move to develop closer economic and political ties.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, hosting the Apeldoorn meeting, said the EU was not ruling anything out and that his colleagues would be considering a number of options.
There were also growing signs that many in the EU believe Albania would be best served if President Sali Berisha quit.
"I'm sure that if President Berisha was to step down that would in some ways improve the situation in Albania," Helveg Petersen said.

Despite having to discuss Albania, the EU ministers were keen to get the issue behind them so they could address some long-term EU issues on the planned agenda, such as enlargement and the relationship with NATO enlargement plans.
On Sunday, ministers were due to turn their attention to relations with Turkey, recently snubbed by Christian Democrat leaders from the EU.
